title: Does Your Politics Decide How You Read the Bible?
subtitle: Each tribe has a canon within the canon. The verses we underline and the verses we explain away tell the truth about who is actually holding the pen.

sections.title: Two Canons, One Bible
sections.body:
Every Christian I know reads the whole Bible. Every Christian I know also has a working canon, the texts that get preached, quoted, and printed on signs, and the working canons sort neatly by party.

The conservative canon runs through Romans 13 on submission to governing authorities, the sexual ethics of Leviticus 18 and Romans 1 and 1 Corinthians 6, and the personal responsibility texts, 2 Thessalonians 3:10, if a man will not work, neither shall he eat. The progressive canon runs through Matthew 25 and the least of these, the Jubilee of Leviticus 25, Luke 4 and good news to the poor, and Amos rolling justice down like waters.

Set the two lists side by side and you'll notice something uncomfortable. Both are Scripture, and neither tribe disputes the other's verses; we just file them differently. Ours are clear commands, and theirs are complicated, contextual, in need of careful handling by experts.

Most of us carry a working canon for years before we can see it. The verses we underline and the verses we explain away map onto our politics with a precision that should embarrass us much sooner than it does.

sections.title: Lens First, Text Second
sections.body:
Both tribes make the same move, lens first and text second.

Jonathan Haidt, no theologian, demonstrated it in the lab. Moral intuition comes first, and reasoning follows after, working not as a judge but as a press secretary. We feel our politics in the gut and send the mind out to find verses, and it always finds them, because Scripture is a long book.

Mark Noll showed the same move at full historical scale. By 1861, devout Americans holding the same Bible and the same plain-sense hermeneutic split into two armies, each certain the text underwrote its cause, and the dispute was settled not by exegesis but by artillery. Noll calls it a theological crisis, and it was one, since the Book could not arbitrate between readers who had already chosen. That ought to haunt every confident proof-texter in this country, and it haunted almost no one.

The move is invisible from inside, because no one experiences himself reading with a lens; we experience ourselves reading plainly while the other side twists. That symmetry, each tribe certain that only the other is captive, is itself the strongest evidence that both are.

sections.title: How the Right Reads Around
sections.body:
Watch the right handle the progressive canon. Matthew 25 gets narrowed: the least of these are Christian missionaries, so the passage is about church solidarity, not the poor as such. There is real scholarship behind that reading, but notice how eagerly the narrowing is received, how it arrives as relief rather than as loss. Jubilee becomes purely ceremonial, fulfilled in Christ, with no abiding word about debt or land or the concentration of wealth. The prophets thundering against those who trample the needy get filed under ancient Israel's covenant, not directly applicable, while the same prophets on idolatry and sexual sin remain timeless.

The technique is consistent. Spiritualize the text, contextualize the text, or kick the verse upstairs into the next life. By every route, the money stays where it was.

Pastors, and I am one, can get good at this. We can exegete a hard saying of Jesus into something a major donor could live with, and call the result balance. That isn't balance. It's a tribe protecting its treasure from its own Scriptures, with a preacher holding the door open.

sections.title: How the Left Reads Around
sections.body:
Now watch the left handle the conservative canon. Romans 13 gets historicized: Paul wrote to a vulnerable house church under particular circumstances, so the call to honor governing authority dissolves whenever the government in question is one we oppose, though it firms up again the moment our side holds power. The sexual ethics texts get assigned to ancient context, trajectory readings, what Paul could not have known. Some of those arguments deserve real engagement on exegetical grounds. But notice, again, how eagerly the conclusion is received, how the scholarship always lands exactly where the surrounding culture already stood. The personal responsibility texts fare worse. They aren't reinterpreted; they just aren't preached.

The technique is the same one, run in reverse. Historicize the text, complicate the text, or kick the verse downstairs into the past. By every route, the autonomy stays where it was.

Preachers hold this door too. Many of us have softened what Scripture says about holiness because the room we wanted to reach found the subject embarrassing, and we called that compassion. Some of it was. Not all of it.

sections.title: When Did a Text Last Change You
sections.body:
So here's the test, and I put it to myself before I put it to you. When did a passage of Scripture last change your politics? I don't mean confirm them. Change them, so that it cost you a position, an alliance, an applause line. If the answer is never, then the Bible isn't functioning as your authority. It's functioning as your wardrobe, and you dress your prior commitments in it every morning.

A better lens won't fix it, since there's no lensless reading, and pretending to one is how we got here. What helps is a willing lens, which means reading with your own tribe's canon set aside for a season, sitting under the verses your side explains away, asking God to make the text strange again. James Davison Hunter is right that Christians left and right have collapsed faith into political idiom until the church speaks nothing the culture has not already said. Centrism won't get us back, because it's just a third lens. The way back is submission, the old word, to the whole counsel of God.

Keep a list of texts that have defeated you, verses that took something from you that you wanted to keep. Mine would be short, and it should be longer. The same is almost certainly true of yours.
